item.title: The Neurobiological Effects of Trauma
item.description:
Psalm 139:14 (NIV) says, “I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well.” God created us in a manner so intricate that we are still figuring out how our physical and emotional being is affected by our nutrition, nature, nurture, environment, family, childhood, development, relationships, society, and trauma.

Made by God

While we all have similar characteristics, we are also unique. There is no one else like us. Our life is completely our own, designed by God but impacted by the will He allows us to use, as well as the will of others that can positively or negatively affect us. Trauma has a dramatic impact on how God’s design works in us.

When I was a teen, there was a lot that was difficult going on in my life. This caused many emotions, including worry, some fear, and sadness. This happened during the winter months in the mountains of Montana, where I grew up. I remember sitting in our trailer living room, looking out at the giant snowflakes falling in the field and trees outside.

It occurred to me that God, Creator of the universe, cared enough to intricately design each snowflake so that no two are alike. If God cared about the finite details of an infinite universe, then He cared about me, a minute part of His vast creation. No matter what happened, my God was still in control. While all that was going on might not turn out as I chose, He was still there. This is true in the good times and the traumatic times.

What things do we define as trauma? They are events that most people typically picture as “horror movie” type scenarios; however, this is not the only trauma that people experience.

When a traumatic event happens, it can significantly change our trajectory, our ability to cope, adapt, or even function depending on our own level of resilience and what is going on in our lives at the time: personally (life/career), socially (friends/family), or even biologically (medical illness, stress, insomnia, etc.). Traumatic events that affect us can happen at any time in our lives. No one is immune to them.

“Big T” and “Little t” Trauma

The events that we frequently think of as traumatic are what we call “Big T” trauma, but there are also events that are called “Little t” traumas. We picture a Big T trauma as a life-threatening situation: terrorist attack, abuse, rape, combat, major disaster, death of a significant relationship, or witnessing the violent death of someone.

“Little T” traumas can include being bullied, assaulted, a relationship ending, a near-miss event – such as avoiding a major car accident, emotional abuse, or gaslighting. A trauma is defined as any event that causes a significant emotional response, makes you feel unsafe, leaves you feeling less than you are or unworthy, or triggers a survival response in the parasympathetic nervous system: fight, flight, freeze, or fawn.

Fawn is the lesser-known trauma response. It is when a victim tries to appease his or her abuser to make the abuse stop. This involves going along with or agreeing to whatever is said regardless of whether he or she believes it or not.

Indirect Trauma

Many of us have dealt with trauma at some point in our lives. Some of us have had more than our fair share. Trauma can be experienced in both direct and indirect or vicarious situations. Many healthcare professionals, mental health workers, first responders, etc., can experience vicarious trauma through dealing with the victims and being told about the traumas they have experienced.

I once had to provide psychological first aid to a language translator who had to translate the horror my patient had experienced in their violent home country. Hearing what the patient had gone through caused a visceral reaction.

One thing we don’t often consider is that trauma can even affect us in utero. If a pregnant mother went through high-stress situations, trauma, or anything that prompted her neurobiology into a traumatic response, the unborn child absorbs, reacts to, and is affected in the same manner as if we were directly involved in the trauma.

When my mom was pregnant with me, it was a “geriatric” pregnancy because she was thirty-eight in the early 1970’s. She went through many stressful situations during her pregnancy, including the anger of my teenage siblings at the presence of a new baby, and the possibility that my brother had a brain tumor.

During this time, my father suffered a work injury involving ruptured discs two months prior to my birth, experienced a subsequent failed back surgery one month before my birth, and faced the possibility of permanent disability, which became reality one month after I was born. My mom had to go back to work to support our family two weeks after I was born.

This all led to my parasympathetic nervous system increasing and has led to my exaggerated startle response that still affects me five decades later. I jump at the slightest sound, including when the toaster pops up. I’m not scared, but I cannot stop my startle reflex. This amused my college roommates, who would demonstrate they could tell me what they were going to do, like saying “boo,” and I would still jump even though I knew it was coming.

After seeing a movie that I enjoyed, I was excitedly telling my friends at dinner how much I enjoyed it, and it made me jump. One of my friends teasingly responded, “Yeah, but you jump at the credits.” All because in utero trauma heightened my parasympathetic nervous response.

Varied Reponses to Trauma

Why does trauma affect us so differently, and what impact can it have? Many people experience repeated significant traumas and never develop PTSD (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder). Some people will develop PTSD from “Little T” traumas.

The impact of traumatic events can be affected by personalities, how we were raised, our ability to see hope, presence of faith or belief in God, ability to forgive, self-esteem, our neurobiology, neurodivergence (such as ADHD, which has been proven to have an increased risk in the development of PTSD), presence of support or lack thereof, our health, our status, training, etc. There are so many different variables that lead to how impactful any given trauma is.

We all have a go-to trauma response. For example, some of us are fighters, others run (flight), and some will mostly freeze. Despite having a typical response, it does not mean that in every circumstance, where our safety or the safety of others is threatened, we will respond in the same manner.

Sometimes when our response is outside our norm, this leaves us feeling shame, doubt in our abilities, weakness, or feeling like a failure. I have worked with both military/veterans and first responders who are highly trained to react a certain way and, at some point, will completely freeze – even though they have trained to respond a certain way.

As mentioned in the first paragraph, there are many factors involved in the way you respond to a trauma and depending on how the many variables are affecting you and/or how many events you’ve had in a short time, your response may be completely different than you expect.

Suffering multiple events in a short amount of time can also lead to more complex trauma reactions, including significant impact on our ability to function. This is why at some point in our life we may have experienced a Big T trauma that did not have as much impact as a Little T trauma might now.

The Biology of Trauma Response

Nonetheless, there are common neurobiological and emotional reactions to trauma that every trauma survivor experiences. When we face a traumatic situation that causes fear, threatens our safety, or triggers a trauma response, biological changes happen in our brain. The amygdala is where our emotional processing/responses, safety or threat detection, emotional memories, and our capacity for appropriate social interactions or ability to read social cues occur.

Our sympathetic nervous system, in our fight, flight, freeze, or fawn responses, comes from the amygdala. When a trauma awakens our amygdala, our emotional responses go into overdrive to ensure our survival. The direct result of any trauma is that the amygdala physically increases in size at the time of the trauma.

This causes the state of constant hypervigilance that any trauma survivor experiences. This is because the amygdala is in overdrive and does not shut off due to its enlarged size. It is in a constant state of trying to detect and determine if our life is threatened.

Our amygdala starts telling us that we should fear everything. This is why after a trauma has proven our vulnerability, we doubt our ability to determine who or what is safe anymore. When you become a “wounded nail,” everything looks like a hammer.

When your amygdala increases in size and goes into overdrive, the prefrontal cortex goes offline. The prefrontal cortex is where our higher-level thinking, problem-solving, prioritizing, decision-making, and logical responses occur. This is why when you become emotional or afraid, it is quite difficult for you to solve a problem or react in a logical manner.

You cannot see the big picture when your amygdala is on alert. This is why someone with PTSD becomes much more emotionally reactive than they were before the trauma occurred, and it can lead to highly impulsive and erratic behaviors, emotional dysregulation or overreacting to a situation, increased anger, rage, emotional and physical outbursts, inability to trust, and a constant state of fear and anxiety that they are never safe – even with those they love.

Other increases in our body include our startle response (as I have experienced in utero), cortisol levels – our stress hormone, adrenaline dumps, inflammation (leading to higher risk for diabetes and autoimmune disorders), blood pressure, higher resting heart rate, faster respiration, weight gain, and the kindling of our stress response system in our brain called the HPA Axis.

The HPA Axis is the connection between the hypothalamus in the brain that senses stress, the pituitary gland below the brain, and adrenal glands on top of the kidneys. These three glands produce various chemical responses to alert our stress response and subsequent reactions when a trigger happens.

The HPA Axis (or stress response system) reacts to even less stressors than before the trauma. This involves a trigger that reminds you of your trauma, stimulating the axis into action, resulting in the cortisol release that activates your energy levels so you can respond to the threat appropriately (fight/flight) for survival.

The increase in cortisol results in an increase in blood sugar and blood pressure, sending blood to your muscles so you can respond. It is this system and the increase in your amygdala that leads to higher emotional reactions or heightened reactivity to triggers that remind you of your trauma and lead to a more significant reaction to the trigger than you may have had during the initial trauma.

With these neurobiological increases, there are also decreases. The parasympathetic nervous system’s ability to calm you and release sleep hormones is decreased, leading to insomnia, which also leads to higher resting heart rates, higher blood pressure, and difficulty calming yourself. It also includes a decrease in the volume of the hippocampus, as well as a decrease in short-term memory recall.

The hippocampus is a small part of the brain located in the temporal lobe of both hemispheres and is part of the limbic system. The limbic system is the part of our brain that includes the amygdala we discussed previously. It also includes the cingulate gyrus, where our brain links our behaviors to outcomes and pain, resulting in our behavioral reactions when something reminds us of or triggers our trauma responses.

When we experience trauma, our hippocampus decreases in size. This part of the brain’s responsibility is in memory making (sorting and changing short-term into long-term), spatial reasoning (our map system – allowing us to learn physical spaces and routes), and contextual reasoning (linking our memories with emotions and sensory input that occurred while the memory was being implanted).

In Alzheimer’s and dementia, it is the part of the brain that is damaged first. In trauma, the shrinking of this part of the brain affects our memory of the trauma and stores the various occurrences our senses experienced during the trauma to be emblazoned in our minds.

This is why smell, sound, music, touch, or any other sense involved will bring us right back to the trauma, causing a flashback and reliving the experience as if it is currently happening. It is also why, when those triggers happen, our reactions are even stronger than when the initial trauma happened.

It also causes the corpus collosum to shrink. The corpus collosum allows the left and right hemisphere of the brain to send data back and forth, as well as aids in the ability of the hemispheres to communicate with regards to memory aides. In addition, it causes the volume of the brain to shrink overall.

This is especially true when trauma happens in childhood because the emotional and physical development of the brain is stunted. The corpus callosum allows the integration of logical thought from the left hemisphere to communicate with the emotional processing of the right hemisphere.

The decrease in the corpus callosum affects the communication between our logical and emotional processing, causing dysfunction in our responses, word recall, ability to make rational decisions, and emotional dysregulation (mood swings, regulated emotional reactions, etc.), as well as decreasing our ability to cope with stress.

Various Reactions

When trauma happens, we do our best to stop thinking about it, thus avoiding the pain and memories that it inflicts. Avoidance can come in many different forms, including keeping busy by throwing ourselves into our work or school. Not talking about it or acting like it never happened. Compartmentalizing so we can continue doing what we need to do, especially if the trauma is part of our job.

It can also lead to maladaptive ways such as turning to drugs or alcohol, gambling, sex, or other addictions to treat the symptoms (such as insomnia), avoid the emotions, or feel something other than numbness. It tricks us into thinking we are over the trauma. Avoidance will work for a while, but only for so long. The duration of avoidance differs from person to person. However, eventually that time runs out.

You have noticed that little things start to bother you more. You get angry at the slightest provocation. You become easily enraged. Have difficulty controlling it and lash out in ways that is uncharacteristic. Anxiety increases, bringing along panic attacks and a constant state of fear. You never feel safe, even around your loved ones. You internalize everything as being your fault, believe everyone hates you, or are afraid that everyone is going to abandon you.

You feel less comfortable in public places. Become hypervigilant – jumping at the slightest sound, keeping your head on a swivel, trying to see where the next threat may be coming from. Risky behaviors increase, and your care about your own life decreases. In every situation, you are quick to find the fastest exit point.

Then it feels safer to start isolating and withdrawing from everyone. Your world becomes smaller until you retreat to your home or bedroom. Flashbacks of the trauma start, and nightmares interrupt your sleep. You get to the point where you’re afraid to even go to sleep and do things to keep yourself awake.

You’re not losing your mind; it is your trauma starting to resurface. You thought it was gone, but avoidance does not make the trauma go away. It makes it lurk in the shadows, festering and growing, like an infection, until it can no longer be contained.

So many of my patients have come to me wondering why their emotions start to betray them, behaviors become uncharacteristic, family relationships become strained, mistrust is rampant, overthinking and overanalyzing every situation means the brain forgets how to rest or be quiet, the body goes into a constant state of vigilance, anxiety becomes a constant companion, every scenario you play in your mind has a catastrophic end.

Maladaptive behaviors (addiction, excess risks) start to envelop your life, leading to new problems and further relationship strain.

Your Trauma

This, my friend, is your trauma. It has been hidden as long as it is willing to be. It’s time to deal with it, face it, feel it, hurt from it, and process it. While the situation feels hopeless, your life has seemingly fallen apart, and you have reached the end of your rope. There is help. You now understand that what you’re experiencing has neurobiological explanations.

You are not beyond help – you are not crazy! You have been wounded, and it is time for that wound to heal. You see, when God reveals, He is ready to heal. Isaiah 41:10 (NIV) “So do not fear, for I am with you; do not be dismayed, for I am your God. I will strengthen you and help you; I will uphold you with My righteous right hand.”

It is time to start processing through that trauma you have been avoiding. It is time to face fears, emotions, and pain. It is time to seek help. Matthew 11:28 (NIV): “Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.” Psalm 46:1 (NIV).

This is not the way your life has to be. You have been in a state of survival for long enough. It is time to claim your life back, to heal, and to learn how to thrive.

Jeremiah 29:11 (NIV) “For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the Lord, “Plans to prosper and not harm you, plans to give you a hope and a future.” Isaiah 40:31 (NIV) “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They will soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary. They will walk and not grow weak.”

item.title: How Separation Anxiety in Relationships Can Shape the Way You Love
item.description:
There is rarely a connection made between separation anxiety and adults. Most of the time, this behavior is associated with toddlers or young children when they are dropped off at daycare or school. But there is another place where this

anxiety can wreak havoc. Separation anxiety in adult relationships can reshape how an individual loves, communicates, and copes with being away from someone they care about.

They may check a partner’s location constantly and spiral at an unanswered text, leaving them feeling panicked. This isn’t always a drama ploy that seems obvious. This is more like an internal storm that is silently managed for years before anyone notices the actual behavior.

Separation anxiety in relationships doesn’t always trace back to a particular event. It may grow out of an unstable childhood home or parents who were unpredictable in behavior and emotions. There are also origins that are more gradual and come from attachment patterns that were never fully examined. It doesn’t matter where the root actually comes from; the result is a nervous system that reads distance as being dangerous even when nothing is wrong.

Recognizing Separation Anxiety in Relationships

Adults experiencing separation anxiety sometimes feel as though there is a tightening in the chest when a partner, close friend, or family member is out of reach. Often, physical symptoms such as a racing heart or upset stomach happen when separation is coming. They may even notice that they are picking fights right before a partner leaves, as if creating conflict feels safer than sitting with the discomfort of saying bye.

Understanding this in the scope of relationships may sound like a loop of worst-case scenarios. All the what-if questions cycle through the thoughts:

  • What if they don’t come back?
  • What if the silence means something is wrong?
  • What if I am too much?
  • What if they have decided to leave me?

These are thoughts that rarely depict the truth, but they are loud enough to convince someone who struggles with being away from the ones they love. When this pattern is unaddressed, the person experiencing it and the relationship can become worn down. The constant need for reassurance can feel exhausting to a partner who doesn’t understand the force driving it.

Remembering that anxiety distorts perception can provide space to frame a response to this type of anxiety. Scripture speaks many times about this type of fear-driven thinking. God did not create people with a spirit of timidity. He wanted them to have the power, love, and discipline to overcome the anxiety (2 Timothy 1:7).

This doesn’t erase the symptoms or the feelings a person experiences. It offers a place to start in recognizing that fear isn’t the final word on someone’s identity or relationship.

How Attachment Styles Shape the Fear of Distance

When it comes to understanding the ins and outs of separation anxiety, attachment theory can offer a lens that gives sight to a picture most don’t always see. Adults who grapple with anxious attachment regularly crave closeness and reassurance. Their interpretation of normal and healthy independence is a threat.

If their partner needs space to relax after a hard day’s work, they may be triggered to think that there is something wrong with the relationship. These disproportionate thoughts create an unfounded truth that fuels an anxious fear.

This is a survival strategy that developed somewhere in the individual’s life. It is how they learned to become aware of potential loss. However, this strategy creates the disconnection the individual fears the most.

Partners are often pushed away because of the constant and overwhelming need for reassurance. Once this happens, an individual who struggles with separation anxiety has had their worst fears confirmed: they have been left alone. It is a vicious cycle that reinforces itself until someone decides to intentionally interrupt it.

Christian counselors frequently see this in couples who are confused about why the same argument continues to surface. One feels smothered, and the other feels on edge. Neither set of feelings is wrong, but there is a misunderstanding of the attachment that creates the chaos. Once it is identified and named, there is relief. The language to converse about it is no longer shameful.

How Faith Can Steady an Anxious Heart

Faith is not the quick fix for anything, and that includes separation anxiety in relationships. Still, it does provide space to create something that anxiety cannot provide: a foundation that is not dependent on anyone’s presence. Anchoring security on a partner’s proximity makes that person responsible for managing a fear that isn’t theirs to fix.

Scripture points toward a different source of security. A trust in the Lord with all one’s heart, and not leaning into the understanding of the world or self, creates a space to build a new foundation that is stable and concrete on the acknowledgment of who God is and how He will make sure the path is straight (Proverbs 3:5-6).

This is not a promise that says for people to stop needing each other or to stop valuing relationships. This is an invitation to move into an intimate place of ultimate security that allows other relationships to be enjoyed.

Learning how to reframe thoughts around this Scripture is not an easy task, but it will make a difference in how separation is handled. It takes practice to be able to step away and have moments of prayer in the middle of a panic. Journaling through an anxious thought before reacting to it allows for a better response and less need for assurance. It is not an overnight fix, but it is doable with the right support.

Practical Steps Toward Managing Separation Anxiety in Relationships

Naming the patterns of separation anxiety is the first place to start looking for the practical steps that will guide the journey of overcoming it. When a person identifies the anxiety for what it is and not as their relationship falling apart, there is a sense of distance from the fear that begins to take shape. After that initial step, the building of grounding techniques can begin. Slow breathing and naming five things of the senses become the avenues of pause in the middle of the panic.

Having a partner who isn’t afraid to communicate about the situation helps an individual learn how to respond to the anxiety. Patience over confusion and frustration makes space for true conversations that explain and define the truth and dismiss the fear. This honesty will build the intimacy in the relationship that anxiety weakens.

Christian counselors are trained to help individuals develop tools that include practical coping skills and deeper work about the origin of the fear. When therapy meets spiritual practices such as prayer and Scripture meditation, sustainable relief is within reach. Together, these skills address the nervous system’s reaction and the beliefs that feed it.

Progression within the walls of separation anxiety has no designated process or path. Patience is the driving force that can steer the journey toward healing and hope, rather than the cliff. There will be easy days, and there will be hard days. Regardless of the day, retraining the response to the fear is the pathway forward.

The Next Step from Here

Separation anxiety in relationships can feel isolating. It seems as though everyone is moving through goodbyes and distance without issues. This struggle is real, and it is common. It will respond to the right combination of faith, support, and tools. The good news is that no one has to carry this fear alone.

If you feel like this pattern is describing how you face time apart from your loved one, reach out for the right support. Christian counselors offer a space for you to explore the anxiety and its origin without concern for judgment. With the right counselor helping you learn the right strategies, you can overcome the fear of being apart and celebrate when you are back together.

The front office can take your call and connect you with the right counselor so you can begin your journey. We have a reception team that understands the need for connection when you feel as though you are alone in the chaos of anxiety. Call to learn how a counselor can help you.

item.title: Christianity and Culture: The Danger of Overspiritualizing Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety is an insidious liar. It has a unique way of making every thought that passes through your mind, even the most bizarre and unlikely, feel urgent and terrifyingly real. As if anxiety alone isn’t enough to nearly cripple your life, there’s an even greater danger. When you’re a Christian, the struggle can be more in-depth because anxiety can affect your spiritual life. It’s important to pay attention to this intersection between Christianity and culture.

Your Vivid Imagination

That imagination God gave you, the one that lets you paint, write, and come up with creative solutions, can also work against you if you have anxiety.

It’s great to exercise your brain to imagine a complicated storyline or to create a masterful piece of art. But if you have anxiety, that creative mind can also be the thing that starts you spiraling in an unhealthy direction.

Instead of thinking of lyrics to a song, anxiety forces your brain into catastrophizing benign or neutral events. Instead of dwelling on a spine-tingling ending for your first novel, your anxious brain begins to focus on potential future scenarios that don’t look so bright.

When you’re a Christ-follower, and you believe that God can and does speak to His people in quiet and beautiful ways, it can be difficult to decipher where your imagination stops and God’s warnings begin. Christianity and culture can clash, leaving you confused.

Warnings from God About Anxiety in Christianity and Culture

When an anxious thought shoots into your mind, your first instinct is to try to put it into context. Is this just a far-fetched thought? Is this worst-case scenario the most likely outcome? Is this a warning from God?

When anxiety speaks, it demands attention. It delivers messages that are both convincing and urgent. For a Christian who genuinely wants to be sensitive to God’s leading, it can feel almost irresponsible not to take every alarming thought seriously.

One of the most unfortunate attributes of anxiety is that it doesn’t care about the truth. It doesn’t filter out what is real or likely from the catastrophic, unlikely outcomes. Because anxiety hijacks your imagination, your anxious thoughts can present as very real.

When these thoughts strike, and you try to contextualize them, perhaps you consider whether or not they are from God in the process. If you start treating every anxious thought as a potential divine warning, you can get very confused. This confusion doesn’t just affect your emotions, but it can have serious consequences for your spiritual life as well.

Does God Warn His People?

God can absolutely warn His people. That’s not in question. He warned Joseph in a dream to flee Egypt with Mary and Jesus to escape Herod and later told him when it was safe to return. So, knowing that God has a track record of warning people is a given. But if you’re anxious, you might get confused as to exactly what your brain is producing and what God is saying. This discrepancy can be very disorienting.

There’s a significant difference between the Holy Spirit’s quiet conviction and anxiety’s relentless, spinning catastrophizing. God leads you to clarity and action that is supported by God’s good nature and Scripture. Anxiety leads you deeper and deeper into a confusing spiral with no clear way out. But in the fog of anxiety, it can be difficult to decipher the origins of the message.

Spiritual Misattribution

When you spiritualize your anxiety, a few things start to happen almost immediately. Here are some examples of things you may experience when you misattribute spiritual things to anxiety.

Discernment or Fear?

A dangerous consequence of overspiritualizing anxiety is that the fear that your anxiety produces can disguise itself as wisdom. If you are a chronic overthinker and an eager Christ follower, there’s a risk that the in the process of anticipating disaster, your brain may confuse this need for action as God’s warning, not a byproduct of anxiety that it truly is.

Lack of Faith

You may begin to interpret your anxiety itself as evidence of a spiritual failure. Instead of seeing anxiety as the human struggle, born of biology and learned behavior, that it is, you might dub it as evidence of a failed relationship with God.

If you believe your lack of faith is directly evidenced by your anxiety, then you might feel a sense of shame every time you have an anxious thought. Not only are you wrestling with the anxiety itself, but now you’re battling the condemnation and shame from it too.

Distorted View of God

When your anxiety begins to overtake your spiritual life, it can distort your view of God Himself. Instead of viewing Him as a loving and compassionate Father, you might start seeing Him as a distant being who is constantly disappointed and just waiting for you to fail.

In these moments, you start viewing God as an unpredictable communicator. You might think He drops terrifying, ambiguous hints of future catastrophes, leaving it up to your already exhausted mind to not only decode but react to or prevent. This in turn creates a hypervigilant faith. You feel like you’re walking on eggshells just trying to appease a god who values panic rather than resting in the arms of your faithful, loving Father.

Balance Christianity and Culture by Breaking Free

If you find yourself trapped in a cycle of spiritual misattribution, the good news is that you can break free. Once you separate your anxiety from your spiritual discernment, you can begin to see the difference between a misfiring nervous system and the voice of God.

Here’s how to start:

Test the Thought

Anxiety and the Holy Spirit often produce very different patterns, and learning to distinguish between them can help stop spiraling thoughts.

Anxiety is often urgent and chaotic, convincing you that danger is imminent, but unnervingly vague about what exactly you’re supposed to do about it. It often demands immediate attention but offers no concrete or logical path. It likes to keep the question of “What If?” at the forefront of the conversation and thrives in confusion and loves isolation.

The voice of the Holy Spirit, however, leads toward clarity, purposeful action, and restoration. Even when the Spirit convicts sharply, it comes with a sense of truth and a clear path forward. It is accompanied by peace and is supported by Scripture. (This offers another reason to hide those Scriptures in your heart!)

When an unidentified thought crosses your mind, test it against the nature of God. Pray and ask for discernment and confirmation. God is not trying to confuse or trap you, and He is faithful to guide His people with love and wisdom.

Consider the Biology

God created the human body with an intricate and complex nervous system.

When your body enters fight-or-flight mode, your brain is doing what it was designed to do under perceived threat. It pumps cortisol and adrenaline to prepare for the battle. If you have anxiety, this internal warning system is incredibly sensitive and can misfire.

Simply knowing that there is a biological explanation for your anxious symptoms can push you towards getting professional mental health help.

Therapy

Therapy can be incredibly helpful for Christians who are struggling with anxiety. It provides a designated place where you can sort through fearful thoughts before you assign spiritual meaning to them. A good therapist can also help you recognize patterns of catastrophizing and challenge those persistent irrational fears.

While your anxiety might be affecting your spiritual life, the roots are likely planted in biological tendencies and past trauma that your nervous system has learned to respond to. When you follow the trail of your anxiety back to these roots, you and your therapist can begin to identify the causes, and it’s easier to understand the beliefs and triggers that are also tied to your anxiety.

If you’re a believer who also suffers from anxiety, call our office today. Together with your therapist, you can deal directly with your anxiety and begin to understand the spiritual implications that go with it. Soon you will be able to separate your spiritual life from your physical reality. Through the power of God and therapy, you can break free of the spiritual confusion that you’ve been struggling with.

Photo:
“Holding a Bible,” courtesy of Kelly Sikkema, Unsplash.com, CCO License

The post Christianity and Culture: The Danger of Overspiritualizing Anxiety appeared first on Spokane Christian Counseling.

item.title: Social Media and Mental Health: What Doomscrolling Does to the Christian Mind
item.description:
What starts as an innocent look at the news or social media feed to catch up on the latest conversations often stretches into hours. The content shifts from interesting to heavy, alarming, and hard to put down. This is called doomscrolling. It is the compulsive habit of consuming negative, distressing content.

The conversations around social media and mental health are becoming a more serious topic. For believers, it is much deeper than screen time. It is a situation that affects the mind, the soul, and the daily practice of peace meant to be cultivated by faith. This is particularly important when we consider how God calls us to protect our thoughts:

Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. – Romans 12:2, ESV

The Pull Is Real: Understanding Social Media and Mental Health

Scrolling works in a way that appears to be engineered. Platforms are designed to keep users engaged. The algorithms that power them learn to provoke outrage and fear in users. It is not just a lack of discipline, but also a reflection of how these systems are built and the social pressures that come with disconnecting.

Today’s culture leans toward big fan bases and huge numbers of followers, making disconnection feel like negligence. Culture says we’re staying informed, and that means we are responsible. This results in a mindset where stepping away feels like falling behind or not caring.

There is a link between heavy social media use and high rates of anxiety, depression, and emotional exhaustion. It is a cycle that builds on itself. When an individual scrolls more, their nervous system becomes more activated. This results in a struggle to feel settled after scrolling for long periods. Physically, it leads to a mental fog that’s difficult to shake, even though the phone has been put down for hours.

Christian counselors can identify this pattern as a steady erosion of peace that accumulates slowly until its absence becomes impossible to ignore. What may have started as a habit has become a weight that rarely announces what it is doing. Instead, we should focus on the things described in Scripture:

Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable, if there is any excellence, if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things. – Philippians 4:8, ESV

The Christian mind was not built for this

God’s Word teaches about the importance of guarding the mind and instructs us to renew it and set it on things above. But today’s digital culture pushes a more dominant message in the opposite direction. It is an unspoken expectation that says looking away is being uninformed, uncaring, and complicit.

This message sets up a difficult balance for the Christian who wants to stay engaged but also feels called to protect their inner life, which depends on faith. This is a real dilemma that signals something significant is being asked of the mind.

The human brain was not created to process this unrelenting stream of global suffering, breaking news, or comparisons. The constant exposure to distressing content leads to numbness rather than compassion. It creates exhaustion and a quiet kind of despair that settles as people absorb the narratives from their feeds.

The world can reshape perceptions, other people, and even a person’s view of God. The unrelenting, disparaging news does not lead to a perception defined by faith. Instead, it slowly feeds information that keeps us questioning until the damage has already been done. This does not lead to the peace we find in Christ.

You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. – Isaiah 26:3, ESV

How Social Media and Mental Health Patterns Take Root in Daily Life

Doomscrolling slides into the early-morning moments before the day begins and breaks in during the gaps between tasks. It walks into the quiet spaces that once held prayer, reflection, and stillness, and before long, it has become the default. Before a conscious thought, the hand reaches for a phone, and the result is a reactive rhythm of life. The soul is not allowed to be still long enough to find its footing, and there’s no margin left to breathe.

The demand to stay connected competes with staying centered. It builds pressure that is difficult to name but easy to feel. Individuals go to bed carrying heavier weight than when they woke up. The stories and images that have accumulated throughout the day have become lodged in the mind and soul, with nowhere to go.

Christian counselors are trained to work with anxiety and feelings of being digitally overwhelmed. They emphasize that the problem is rarely a single piece of content, but rather the cumulative effect of hours of low-grade emotional input from doomscrolling. The mind was not meant to be consumed by this constant barrage of information. It was designed to be cultivated through healthy and positive interactions with the world and the people in it.

With help, we can be reminded to “Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.” (Colossians 3:2, ESV) This is where we find the peace we long for, not on our feeds or news cycles.

Reclaiming the Mind Through Faith and Intentional Practice

Choosing to step back from doomscrolling doesn’t mean you don’t want to be informed or that you are withdrawing from the world. It is a conscious choice to reinforce the capacity to show up with clarity, compassion, and grounded faith.

By setting boundaries and limits on online habits, an individual can exercise stewardship over a mind given by God. It is an intentional decision to tend to the inner life, with faith that asks for the godly, even as the rest of the culture is still scrolling.

There are practical steps that can make a big difference, such as setting a specific time for scrolling news, removing apps from the home screen, or choosing Scripture and prayer before the first scroll. These are small, consistent choices that can change the feelings and trajectory of the day.

Christian counselors are an avenue of support for this process when anxious scrolling is connected to patterns of fear or a need to control things. The road is really simple, but it is one that faith knows. One step at a time, with a focus on something steady rather than a newsfeed, leads to a quieter mind and a better understanding of what peace should truly be.

You don’t have to do it alone

The digital world and the life of the mind are a way that’s more than a simple lifestyle issue. For Christians, it can be a spiritual one, where the mind takes in and shapes, with the heart, what it believes. This becomes a lifestyle that reflects how an individual lives day to day.

Doomscrolling feeds on comparison, fear, and a lack of hope. A Christian mind anchored in a God who is not rattled begins to understand that His peace extends beyond anything a human mind can comprehend. It is a discovery that His purposes are not undone by anything trending in the newsfeed.

To reclaim the mind takes work that doesn’t happen in a single decision or a weekend without screens. Reclaiming happens in the daily practice of choosing where an individual directs their attention. It is a reflection of purposefully choosing what to feed the soul and who to trust with the weight of the world. This type of faithfulness is quiet and not glamorous, but it is what a renewed mind looks like in the digital age.

In doing this, we can experience the kind of peace we long for:

And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:7, ESV

If you feel that you are engulfed in patterns of digital anxiety and emotional exhaustion connected to online habits, you’re not alone. Many individuals are finding the same battle. If you would like more information, you can contact our office today, and our reception team will connect you with support. You can make an informed decision on the next step toward healthier social media habits.

https://psychcentral.com/anxiety/what-is-doomscrolling

https://www.webmd.com/balance/what-is-doomscrolling
https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/the-dangers-of-doomscrolling/
https://positivepsychology.com/doomscrolling/

item.title: When The Nervous System Is Listening: How Trauma Shapes Communication, Interpretation, and Connection
item.description:
Too often we don’t listen with our ears alone; sometimes our history is listening, too. Having a history of trauma can affect you in more ways than just your memories, emotions, relationships, personality, and inability to move on. One of the ways that trauma will affect your relationships is through communication.

How Communication Works

Communication is not just received through our ears by the direct words of another person. It is filtered through our nervous system, past experiences, trauma, expectations for safety, potential threats, and meanings.

This includes hidden agendas, perceptions, as well as the meanings a person has learned to attach to the words being said by another person, such as their tone, facial expressions, and behaviors. Non-verbal communication is about 90% of all our communication, and it is read through our past experiences, most notably our trauma as interpreted by our nervous system.

Trauma affects not only what a person communicates to others, but it is also impacted by what their nervous system permits them to hear, interpret, retain, and respond to. The trauma suddenly becomes the filter that everything is passed through. A trauma survivor will often receive a different message from the one that is being sent, but it also interprets the intention behind it.

For example, have you ever played the game of telephone? A message is whispered from one to another and then translated to the next person repeatedly until it reaches the last one in the room. What’s left is a message that is nothing like the original that was stated.

This is a prime example of how communication is both translated, filtered, and received differently from one person to another based on a multitude of factors, most significantly the trauma filters involved in receiving communications. Those filters can include fears of rejection, abandonment, being held responsible/blamed, being a burden, feelings of worthlessness, etc.

Trauma and Communication

In all communication, there is a difference between what has been said and what has been received. This includes the speaker’s intent, delivery, and the receiver’s interpretation. Trauma can result in widening the distance between the two. For instance, your partner may say, “We need to talk.”

Their intent may be: “I’m concerned about you,” “You seem to not be yourself,” or “I know you’re hurting.” What you, as the trauma-affected receiver, hear is: “I’m in trouble, it’s my fault, you’re going to leave me, I’m a burden, I’m an embarrassment, I’m always the problem.” The interpretations don’t change the literal words that are said, but the meaning assigned to them becomes completely different.

When shame is listening, correction can sound like condemnation. Often one of the primary trauma filters that is in place is shame. Once shame enters the conversation, the person may defend against a perceived attack on identity rather than respond to the actual concern. Shame becomes a significant factor in any trauma because shame attacks our character.

Shame says, “If I did something bad or something bad was done to me, I am bad.” Shame then becomes the filter through which all communication is sifted, and it clouds the interpretation of what has been said and what has been received. Much of what will be discussed throughout this article can be blamed on that shame filter distorting what is heard.

When shame attacks character, any communication that is filtered through it becomes an arrow that delivers more confirmation of that shame. Some of the previous examples were: “It’s my fault,” “I’m a burden,” “I’m always the problem,” which are all received through a lens of shame that reinforces that you are bad.

Trauma and the Brain

Trauma affects our feelings of safety and causes us to doubt our ability to detect and determine threats. Trauma does substantial damage to our threat-detection system and increases the size of our amygdala, causing it to fire rapidly and be on high alert to potential threats.

The amygdala is where your fight/flight/freeze response is enacted; your emotions become highly reactive, and your brain’s alarm system goes into overdrive, telling you everything is a threat. The prefrontal cortex is where your logic and reasoning power reside, and it sends signals to your amygdala, telling it there is no reason to be alarmed.

Before the trauma, your prefrontal cortex was able to send logic to your alarm system in the amygdala, telling it that there is no reason to be concerned about what is happening because you were safe. This connection becomes damaged and stops sending communications. Your amygdala constantly tells you a threat is happening, and your prefrontal cortex cannot tell it to calm down.

In essence, you become the wounded nail, and everything around you is a hammer waiting to inflict more pain. This breaks down your ability to logically reason and listen to the literal words being told to you. Your amygdala tells you there is a hidden message in them that reinforces your fears that you are in danger.

That hidden message tells you that your worst fears are true. You are about to get in trouble, it’s your fault, you will be abandoned, or you are a burden to everyone around you. The constant alarm system of your amygdala inhibits your brain’s ability to calm or soothe you and tells you the trauma is happening again, or a new trauma is occurring.

If you think about when you have been in a building where a loud fire alarm is going off, it is hard to focus on anything around you or hear instructions. Your amygdala is that fire alarm in your brain that is constantly overriding any other information coming through.

Trauma teaches the brain that to stay safe, you must prioritize threat detection because the trauma has taught you that your ability to detect what is safe can no longer be trusted. Specifically, when your past has involved repeated danger, criticism, abuse, unpredictability, betrayal, or abandonment, your brain becomes exceptionally skilled at searching for signs that something bad is coming.

Interpretation of Communication

What this means is that everyday conversations or even the slightest hint of conflict will be examined as danger without being able to process the true meaning or words being said.

If your partner has a neutral facial expression, you will automatically interpret it as anger. Instead of them just thinking about something else. A delayed text means rejection. Instead of an interruption. A sigh is irritation or disapproval, meaning you’re a burden or it’s your fault, instead of them thinking about the long list of tasks still to do at work or that they didn’t sleep well.

Every little gesture, behavior, expression, or action is interpreted as if you are the cause or at fault. “Why did you say that?” is interpreted as “You’re a monster.” “I wish you would have done [something]” is heard as “It’s your fault this happened.”

Tone and body language become louder than the words being said. Tone is often misinterpreted as having an edge to it. Even when your partner says they are not angry, you interpret that as a lie because you’re hyper-focused on the tone and non-verbal cues. Your traumatized nervous system will say, “That’s a lie! They’re trying to trick me!”

You’ve become unable to consciously discern or translate any communication as positive because every communication subconsciously reinforces that you’re under attack. This is due to your nervous system constantly performing threat appraisal in everything you see or hear. Your amygdala is telling you that your threat responses are your only option. Your response must be fight, flight, freeze, or fawn (appeasing your attacker).

When your communication activates your trauma response, your ability to calmly process language diminishes. You can’t listen to understand the content or message. Your communication problems with your partner are an inability to regulate emotions/fear or understand the exact meaning of what is being said. That is, they are not failures in communication, but failures in regulation and threat assessment. You have damaged filters.

Trauma Threat Responses

Instead, your nervous system is telling you to go into survival mode, or you won’t make it. In communication, this can occur in one or more of the following ways:

Fight: arguing, defensiveness, anger, disruption, counterattacking.

Flight: leaving the conversation, deflecting, changing the subject, avoiding texts or calls.

Freeze: going blank, becoming silent, dissociating, being unable to answer, shutting down.

Fawn: immediately agreeing, apologizing, appeasing, or saying what the other person wants to hear – even if you disagree [anything to make it stop].

In healthy communication, we listen for meaning without bias. Trauma causes us to listen for danger with extreme prejudice that everything has a hidden meaning and everyone has a hidden agenda. Instead of listening to the words your partner is saying you listen to why this means danger.

Your nervous system constantly asks: “Are they angry? Am I in trouble? Are they criticizing me? Are they going to leave? Am I losing control? Do I need to defend myself? What aren’t they telling me?”

The conclusions you automatically draw are: “I’ve done something wrong again. I’m a failure. They hate me. I can never do anything right. I’m useless. I’m worthless. Why bother? I must defend myself. I’m unsafe. I’m all alone. No one understands me. They would be better off without me.”

Once your internal threat monitor goes off, you lose the ability to clearly discern what is being said. Everything you hear from then on is filtered through your trauma and past negative experiences. It’s as if everyone from your past suddenly is standing behind your partner, shouting all the defeating and threatening thoughts your nervous system is interpreting.

Your ability to rationally listen to the content and truth is completely disconnected. It’s like someone has pulled the plug on your prefrontal cortex and pushed the gas pedal on your amygdala. All rational thought has left the building. Suddenly your present conversation becomes connected to, or just plain becomes, an old conversation that you have had with more than just your partner. All current meaning, issues, or problems are irrelevant.

The ability to solve the current issue or find any resolution flies out the window. When communicating involves heightened emotions, dredging up the past, or the inability to regulate emotions, it can be nearly impossible to find resolution. Then, when you are not only communicating with your partner but also with those from your past, conflict will only escalate, and a feeling of unsafety, as well as hopelessness for change, will set in.

Ambiguous Communication

Often communication becomes ambiguous, leaving a lot unsaid and open to interpretation. For a person who has not had trauma, that ambiguity is frequently left at face value, and nuances or motives are not read into it. For those with a history of trauma, that ambiguity becomes subject to a whole host of new dangers and threats.

If your partner texts you to “call when you get a chance,” a person without trauma will think, “Sure, as soon as I get a second.” However, for those with a history of trauma, it sends you into a catastrophic spiral that can lead to all kinds of dangerous conclusions.

For example, you will start thinking, “Something is wrong, I did something wrong, they’re angry with me, I’m about to be rejected, they hate me, I can’t do anything right, everything is my fault, they’re going to abandon me, I’m all alone.” It’s the same six words in a text that have completely different meanings for the person with no history of trauma than the nervous system response for the one with trauma.

Information that is incomplete means the brain has to fill in the missing pieces. Ambiguity means uncertainty, which means unpredictability that leads to danger and worst-case scenarios being played out over and over again in your thoughts.

Rejection, Abandonment, and Boundaries

A history of rejection or abandonment can also complicate how communication is received in the same way that ambiguity does. In communication and relationships, boundaries are essential and healthy. However, to those with rejection or abandonment issues, boundaries mean they are about to relive that all over again.

Setting a healthy boundary before conflict is discussed increases the likelihood of calmer discussions and ultimate resolution. Yet to the person with trauma those healthy boundaries, such as “I can’t talk about this now” or “I need space” or “We’ll talk later.” These boundaries are interpreted as “You’re trying to control me” or “You’re rejecting me” or “You’re leaving me.”

This can produce pursuit, anxious attachment, reassurance seeking, anger, withdrawal, or attempts to control the conversation, which may ironically create the very relational distance the person fears. Trauma-induced catastrophic thinking then creates confirmation loops based on beliefs or stuck points that come from the trauma.

Trauma and Memory

In addition, trauma can also affect memory during conversations due to the nervous system being heightened. When your amygdala has sent out the threat signal, your emotions go into overdrive. The prefrontal cortex goes offline, resulting in every word being heard through emotions and shame. When you are in a heightened emotional state, you have a difficult time storing logical, organized, consecutive memories.

High arousal can interfere with attention, working memory, organization, and encoding of information. Someone may leave a difficult conversation remembering only fragments, especially the most emotionally threatening pieces. Two people can therefore walk away with strikingly different memories of the same discussion.

This doesn’t mean that neither party was listening. It means that neither party was hearing the same conversation. The trauma-affected brain prioritizes information in association with what is necessary for survival rather than context.

Furthermore, a common coping mechanism that results from trauma is dissociation. This happens to separate the victim from the trauma to protect them from what is happening. This becomes a response the brain becomes attached to and fond of. If I separate my conscious mind from what is happening around me, I don’t have to experience what is happening, and then I don’t have to relive it later.

Dissociation can become such an unhealthy coping mechanism that the slightest hint of conflict, stress, triggers, or danger can result in being mentally checked out from reality. If the brain is off in another world, memories of what is currently occurring cannot be stored. If I’m not aware of what is happening, I can believe I am safe.

Dissociation can start occurring so frequently that you become less in touch with reality and start to isolate yourself in your own mental world. To your partner, you may appear calm and listening while internally you are detached, numb, foggy, or mentally absent.

You may nod and respond in short statements, like “okay,” but will later have no recollection that the conversation took place. You appear to be compliant and agreeable. However, compliance is not necessarily comprehension. Silence is not listening, and your calm appearance is not you being in control of your emotions.

The Need for Control

Trauma that involves a state of helplessness creates a powerful need for predictability and control. One of the main symptoms or effects of this type of trauma is a need for control in every aspect of your life. “If I am in control, I am safe, and trauma cannot happen to me again. If I am not in control, I am at risk and in danger.”

The need for control starts impacting every area of your life, including your communication. During conversations, this can appear as needing an immediate answer, demanding certainty, repeatedly asking the same question, controlling when or how discussions occur, struggling when someone needs space, or becoming distressed when outcomes remain unresolved.

This also leads to requests or conflict being interpreted as “they’re trying to control me. If I am being controlled, I am going to be hurt again.”

Why Better Communication and Listening Aren’t Always Enough

Now that you are aware of how your nervous system disrupts your ability to receive what is being said, how do we make communication clearer? Traditionally, advice on communication asserts that appropriate words should be chosen, like using “I” statements, not interrupting, listening actively – not being focused on your response while your partner is talking, paraphrasing, and avoiding blame.

However, when your communication has been hijacked by your nervous system and past trauma, these important skills won’t matter. Your nervous system is actively trying to discern how big the threat is, how much danger you are in, and telling you the worst-case scenario is going to happen.

Remember the amygdala and prefrontal cortex? Trauma has broken the ability for those primary parts of your brain to communicate with each other. It has also increased the size of your amygdala, which is constantly on alert and sends signals that a looming threat is in every conversation, facial expression, body language, and tone. With your nervous system being alert, you will not be able to focus on the normal pathways for healthy communication.

So, what do you need to do? Is your communication doomed to misconceptions forever? Not at all! However, there are steps that need to be taken before you can start directly addressing how you perceive communication. You see, when your emotions are dysregulated or unstable, you can’t just choose to control them.

Emotional Regulation

You need to be able to get your emotions regulated and start processing the misconceptions or stuck points you have surrounding your trauma before you will be able to hear the content that is being spoken. This takes therapy.

When someone experiences trauma, one of the most common symptoms that comes from it is avoidance. This is a common problem among most trauma survivors. It is also one of the most dangerous behaviors that inhibits your trauma recovery.

When trauma is avoided, it does not go away. It festers just like an infection and starts to invade every area of your life. This process of festering does not have a specific timeline. For some, it will spread quickly after the trauma, impairing your ability to function. Then you learn how to avoid it, and you become a master at that avoidance. You convince yourself you’ve moved on and the trauma isn’t affecting you.

You tell everyone you are good at compartmentalizing it. It doesn’t bother you. The problem is, like any compartment, it can only hold so much. Initially, it will start by leaking. You develop maladaptive behaviors: overeating, addictions, isolation, too much spending, anger outbursts, etc. You are in denial that there is a trauma root to your behavior.

These maladaptive behaviors start interrupting your relationships, causing issues at work, your anger starts growing, or you are easily overwhelmed at the slightest task. You will slack at work, be constantly late, and call out more frequently. You might start to overreact to situations that are minor and underreact to situations that should be concerning because you don’t care what happens to you.

Eventually the compartment gets too full, and it bursts open. Your relationships start to crumble, your job is at risk – if not lost, your world gets smaller the more you withdraw and isolate. Conflict increases and communication crumbles. Anger and emotions are out of control. You and your family are left wondering what is wrong.

Regulation must happen before resolution can. Recovery through therapy starts with education about what is going on. You may feel like you are crazy, but you’re not. You have been wounded, and it hasn’t been able to heal. Each time you have avoided it, that avoidance has fed it, causing it to grow. Now it is so big it can no longer be avoided. It is time to start processing it, but it doesn’t mean you have to relive it.

Addressing Feelings

You must address how it has made you feel, and the stuck points or misconceptions you have created surrounding it, such as believing it is your fault. Your need for control of everything has gotten to a point of exhaustion.

By working through these stuck points and stopping the constant analysis paralysis of the event, trying to make it more acceptable or understandable as to why it happened. You find that the only thing you have some control over is blaming yourself. If you were responsible, then you could prevent it from happening again.

While you start learning how your trauma has affected you, your partner also needs to be educated on what is going on. Additionally, if your partner has trauma, it adds even more complications to your communication. You each are filtering what is said through your own trauma. Awareness and knowledge provide reassurance and safety that have long been missing.

As awareness increases, as well as your ability to recognize safety, you become more able to regulate your emotions. When your emotions calm down, it means your nervous system starts taking a break. You become more able to feel connection to the ones you love. Then your communication can start improving, and you are better able to solve problems because your prefrontal cortex is brought back online.

Education and knowledge provide a chance for trauma-informed communication. When you and your partner know the barriers and how you each interpret what is being said, you become more prepared to improve your communication.

Trauma-Informed Communication

Trauma-informed communication can involve slowing the interaction, decreasing intensity, using clear rather than ambiguous language, avoiding unnecessary ultimatums, checking what the person heard rather than assuming understanding, allowing processing time, validating emotions without necessarily agreeing with interpretations, maintaining predictable boundaries, and returning to difficult conversations after regulation has been restored.

The most important part of restoring communication is separating emotions from it. If you are angry, emotional, or struggling to control your emotions, do not engage in conflict or try to have conversations about problems if you cannot keep your emotions out of it. When you are emotional, your amygdala is rapidly firing, warning of danger.

This is where boundaries are important. You must establish a period where you can calm down and rationally talk about the problems at hand. You cannot find resolution if you cannot communicate. Once you can calmly discuss the situation, you need to stay on the task at hand. Do not bring up past issues.

As you talk, keep checking in on your emotions and do grounding techniques (breathing exercises, count backwards, things that keep you present and calm). Your nervous system cannot send your amygdala into overdrive if you are trying to solve problems like counting backwards; your prefrontal cortex has to be fully engaged.

As things your partner says start to trigger those feelings of being blamed or things filtered through shame, it is time to clarify. Tell your partner, “This is what I heard you say. Is that what you meant?” These questions can quickly provide clarification for misconceptions and close the gap in communication.

Tell your partner how what they said triggered your feelings and discuss between the two of you what is triggering and find other ways that thoughts might be expressed. When you and your partner can educate each other about the intent behind what is being said, feelings can be expressed, and resolution can occur. Knowing the intent behind a conversation can lead to a greater understanding instead of misunderstanding.

We don’t receive communication with our ears alone. We hear it through the filter of everything we have survived, learned, feared, and come to expect. Sometimes our history is listening too.
